title: Business Logic and Process Automation
summary: Formulas, roll-ups, validation rules and flows: make Salesforce calculate, check and act by itself, with clicks instead of code.

lessons.title: Formula fields and their limits
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, demonstrate the use of formula fields to meet stated business requirements.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **formula field** works out its own value from other fields. Nobody types into it. It is **read-only** and recalculates every time someone looks at the record. Use it when a value always follows a rule, like days until a deadline or a discount price.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A spreadsheet cell with `=B2*0.9` in it. Change B2 and the cell updates by itself. Where it stops: a formula field can't change other fields or records. It only shows its own answer.

cards.title: Pick a return type
items: Every formula has one **return type**: the kind of answer it gives
Checkbox, Currency, Date, Date/Time, Number, Percent, Text or Time
Example: days open is Number. Is it late? is Checkbox

cards.title: A tiny example
cards.body: Shows the days left until the due date, or 0 once the status is Closed.

cards.title: The size limits
items: Up to **3,900 characters** of formula text
Up to **1,300 characters** shown after it runs
Save size and compile size: at most **15,000 bytes** each
No long text area, encrypted or Description fields inside a formula

cards.title: Two rules people forget
cards.body: You can't delete a field that a formula uses. Remove it from the formula first. For a picklist, use `ISPICKVAL()` or `TEXT()`, because a plain `=` comparison won't work on a picklist.

A formula field can't be edited by users, flows or imports. If the business wants a value people can override, use a normal field set by a flow instead. Also: `ISCHANGED()` and `PRIORVALUE()` don't work in formula fields.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Formula = calculator, not a notebook.** It shows an answer. It never stores what you type.

terms.say: A field that works out its own value from other fields, like a calculator cell. Nobody types into it.
You can look at it, but you can't change it.
The kind of answer a formula gives back, like a number, a date, some text or a yes/no tick.
A tick box. It is either true (ticked) or false (not ticked).
A money amount, like 25.00 dollars.
The most letters and symbols you can type into one formula.
The most characters a text formula can show after it runs.
The biggest a formula may get once Salesforce saves and compiles it, behind the scenes.
A formula function that asks: is this picklist set to this exact value? It answers true or false.
A function that gives a field's old value from before this save. It works in validation rules, not formula fields.

lessons.title: Cross-object formulas
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, demonstrate the use of formula fields to meet stated business requirements.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **cross-object formula** reads fields from a related parent record. A Contact formula can show its Account's industry. You write the path with dots: `Account.Industry`. It saves you copying data around, and it always shows the parent's current value.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Asking your mum what your home address is. You don't keep a copy; you look it up each time. Where it stops: you can only look **up** to parents. A parent can't read its children this way.

cards.title: Reading up the chain
cards.body: The first line reads the account owner's email. The second handles an Owner that can be a user or a queue.

cards.title: The rules
items: At most **10 unique relationships** per object, across all formulas, rules and lookup filters
Two formulas using the same path, like opportunity to account, count once
A cross-object formula **can't be used in a roll-up summary**
Tasks and events can't use contact or account merge fields

cards.title: Owner is special
cards.body: Some objects let a **queue** (a shared to-do list a team works from) own records. Then Owner is **polymorphic**: it can point to different object types. Say which one with `Owner:User.` or `Owner:Queue.`. Name fields built from other fields can't be used, like `Owner.Name`.
Need a total of child records, like the sum of all line amounts? A cross-object formula can't look down to children. Use a **roll-up summary** field (master-detail) or a flow instead.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Formulas look up, roll-ups look down.** Dots climb to the parent, and there are only 10 rungs on the ladder per object.

terms.say: A formula that reaches up to a related parent record and shows one of its fields.
A formula path. Start at this record's Account, then read its Industry field.
Each object can use at most 10 different parent paths across its formulas, rules and lookup filters.
A parent field that counts or adds up its child records in a master-detail relationship.
Placeholders that pull a value from a record, like a blank you fill in from the data.
A shared to-do list. A team can own records together until one person picks them up.
A field that can point to more than one kind of object, like Owner pointing to a user or a queue.
Tells a formula: read the owner as a person (a user), not a queue.
Tells a formula: read the owner as a queue, not a person.

lessons.title: Roll-up summary fields
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, determine the capabilities, use cases, and implications of roll-up summary fields.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **roll-up summary field** sits on a parent record. It counts or adds up its child records. An Order can show how many lines it has, or their total. It updates by itself when children change. It needs a **master-detail** relationship (a strong parent-child link).

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A teacher's register that shows the class size and the top score. Add a pupil and the total changes. Where it stops: it only works for a **master-detail** class, not a loose lookup link.

cards.title: Four calculations
items: **COUNT**: how many child records
**SUM**: number, currency or percent fields
**MIN** and **MAX**: those plus date and date/time fields
Add filter criteria to count only some children, like Status = Paid

cards.title: Where you can create one
items: Any custom object on the master side of a master-detail
A standard object that is master of a custom detail object
**Opportunity** from opportunity products
**Account** from opportunities
**Campaign** from campaign members

cards.title: What it can't summarize
items: Auto number fields
Cross-object formula fields
Formulas using `NOW()`, `TODAY()` or `DATEVALUE()`
Limit: **25 roll-up summary fields** per object

cards.title: After you build one
cards.body: Once it exists, you **can't convert** the master-detail into a lookup. You also can't change its detail object. A big recalculation can take up to **30 minutes**. A mass recalculation doesn't fire workflow rules or validation rules. Hidden child fields still count.

cards.title: Cap a parent at 25 children
cards.body: A validation rule on the child. It blocks a new line once the parent's roll-up count reaches 25.
A roll-up summary needs a master-detail. On a **lookup**, the usual answer is a flow instead. You can convert a lookup to master-detail only if every child record already has a parent.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **C-S-M-M: Count, Sum, Min, Max.** Roll-ups roll **up**, and only on a master-detail hill.

terms.say: A parent field that counts or adds up its child records by itself.
A strong parent-child link. The child can't live without its parent and follows its sharing.
Tells you how many child records there are.
Adds up a number field across all the child records.
Finds the smallest value among the child records, like the earliest date.
Finds the biggest value among the child records, like the latest date or the top amount.
Rules that pick which children to include, like only paid invoices.
A field that gives each new record the next number by itself, like a ticket number.
A loose link between records. The child can live alone, and the link can be empty.
When Salesforce redoes a roll-up for many records at once, like after you change its definition.

lessons.title: Validation rules
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, demonstrate the use of validation rules to meet stated business requirements.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **validation rule** stops bad data from being saved. It is a formula that checks the record. If the formula says **TRUE**, the data is bad: Salesforce blocks the save and shows your **error message**. If it says FALSE, the save goes on.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A bouncer at the door. If you break a rule, you don't get in, and the bouncer says why. Where it stops: the bouncer checks every door, not just the front one. Imports and the API get checked too.

cards.title: Close date can't be in the past
cards.body: TRUE (blocked) only when someone changes the close date to a day before today.

cards.title: Where the rule runs
items: Every save: the screen, the **API**, data imports
Even when the checked field is not on the page layout
Not for records made with **Quick Create**
The error shows at the **top of the page** or **next to a field**

cards.title: Handy functions
items: `ISNEW()`: true when the record is being created
`ISCHANGED(field)`: true when the field just changed
`PRIORVALUE(field)`: the value before this save
`ISBLANK(field)`: true when the field is empty
`REGEX()` checks a pattern; `VLOOKUP()` works only in validation rules

cards.title: Let chosen users skip it
cards.body: Some users, like an integration user, must skip a rule. Create a **custom permission**. Put it in a **permission set** (an extra bundle of access you give to chosen users). Check it in the rule with **$Permission**: `NOT($Permission.Bypass_Rules)`. Users without it are still checked.

cards.title: Where it sits in a save
cards.body: When a record saves, **before-save flows** run first. Then Apex before triggers run. Then validation rules check the result. So a field a before-save flow sets is still validated.
The formula describes the **bad** case, not the good one. "Amount must be over 0" becomes `Amount <= 0`. Writing the good case blocks every correct record.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **TRUE means trouble.** The rule fires when the data is wrong.

terms.say: A check that runs when you save. If the data breaks the rule, the save stops and you see a message.
The words a user sees that explain what to fix before saving.
A way for other programs to talk to Salesforce and save data without the normal screens.
An old, small Classic form for making records fast. Validation rules don't check records made with it.
A function that asks: did this field just change in this save? It answers true or false.
A function that asks: is this record brand new right now? It answers true or false.
An on-off switch you invent. You give it to some users, and rules or flows can check who has it.
An extra bundle of access you give to chosen users, on top of their profile.
A formula word that checks whether the current user has a certain custom permission.
Flows that change a record just before it's saved. They run before validation rules check it.

lessons.title: Choosing the right flow type
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, determine the appropriate flow type to meet stated business requirements.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **flow** is automation you build with clicks in **Flow Builder**. The flow type says how the flow starts and whether a person takes part. Choosing the type is the first decision, and the exam tests it a lot.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Alarm clocks. One rings when a door opens (record-triggered). One rings at 7 a.m. (scheduled). One waits for a button press (screen flow). Where it stops: an alarm can't ask questions, but a screen flow can.

cards.title: The core types
items: **Screen Flow**: guides a person through screens
**Record-Triggered Flow**: runs when a record is created, updated or deleted
**Schedule-Triggered Flow**: runs at a set time for a batch of records
**Platform Event-Triggered Flow**: runs when a platform event message arrives
**Autolaunched Flow (No Trigger)**: runs when something calls it

cards.title: Two more you should know
items: **Flow Approval Process**: a multi-step approval built in Flow
**Orchestration**: a multi-step, multi-user process made of stages and steps

cards.title: Who can do what
cards.body: Only a **screen flow** can show screens and use **Choice** resources (options to pick from). Only a **record-triggered flow** can use the **Custom Error** element. An autolaunched flow runs in the background with no screens.
"Ask the user for input" always means a **screen flow**. A record-triggered or scheduled flow can't show a screen, even if a person's save started it.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Who or what starts it?** A person → screen. A save → record-triggered. A clock → scheduled. An event → platform event. A caller → autolaunched.

terms.say: Automation you build by dragging boxes and arrows in Setup, instead of writing code.
The Setup tool where you draw a flow: you add steps and connect them with arrows.
A flow that shows screens to a person and asks them questions.
A flow that runs by itself when a record is created, updated or deleted.
A flow that runs at a set time, once, daily or weekly, for a group of records.
A flow that wakes up when a certain event message arrives, like a sensor alert.
A big process split into stages and steps, where different people and flows each do their part.
A ready-made option a user can pick on a flow screen, like one radio button.
A flow element that stops a save and shows a message you write. Only record-triggered flows have it.

lessons.title: Record-triggered flows: before or after save
lessons.objective: Create and configure flows using Flow Builder.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **record-triggered flow** runs by itself when a record is saved or deleted. In the Start element you pick the object, the event and the **entry conditions** (which records count). Then you pick when it runs: before save or after save.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: Fixing a letter before you post it (before save) versus sending a second letter after it arrives (after save). Where it stops: after save also lets you write to other people, not just fix your own letter.

cards.title: Before save: fast field updates
items: Updates fields on the **same record** that triggered it
Change `$Record` directly; no Update Records element needed
Only **Assignment, Decision, Get Records and Loop**
Runs just before Apex before triggers

cards.title: After save: everything else
items: Create or update **related records**
Run actions: send email, post, call a subflow
Can read the new record's **Id** and system fields like Last Modified Date
Can add **scheduled paths** to run later, like 3 days after a date

cards.title: And before delete
cards.body: A third choice: **before delete**. It runs when a record is about to be deleted, so you can act first or block it with a Custom Error.

cards.title: Run only when it starts to match
cards.body: Entry conditions can run the flow **only when a record is updated to meet the conditions**. That fires once, when the record first starts to match, not on every later edit.

cards.title: Limits
cards.body: Per org: **50 versions** per flow. **2,000 active** and **4,000 total** flows per flow type in Enterprise Edition and above.
"Update a field on the record itself" → choose before save; it's the fastest. "Create a task" or "update the parent account" → before save can't do that, so choose after save.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Before = fix me. After = tell the world.**

terms.say: Rules in the Start element that say which records make the flow run.
The record that started the flow. You can read its fields, and in before save you can change them.
A flow element that sets or changes a value, like writing a number into a box.
A flow element that picks a path, like a fork in the road with an if-this, go-that-way sign.
A flow element that finds records in the database and brings them into the flow.
A flow element that goes through a list one item at a time.
Other records linked to this one, like the account above a contact or the tasks under it.
Parts of a record-triggered flow that wait and run later, like three days after a close date.
A record-triggered flow choice that runs just before a record is deleted.
Each flow can keep up to 50 saved versions. Only one can be active at a time.

lessons.title: Screen flows and where to put them
lessons.objective: Create and configure flows using Flow Builder.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A **screen flow** guides a person step by step. It shows screens with fields, choices and messages. Then it can save records. Use it for a wizard: a guided form that asks questions in order.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A self-checkout machine. It asks one thing per screen and you press Next. Where it stops: each Next starts a new **transaction** (one save job), so earlier screens' saves stay saved.

cards.title: Where users can launch it
items: A **Lightning page**: home, app or record page, with the Flow component
A **flow action**: a quick action button on a record
The **utility bar** at the bottom of an app
A custom button or link, or a web tab
An **Experience Builder** page for site visitors
Inside Aura, LWC or Visualforce

cards.title: Pass the record in
cards.body: To know which record it is on, add a text variable named `recordId`. Mark it **Available for input**. On a record page or flow action, Salesforce fills it with the record's Id.

cards.title: Who can run it
cards.body: Most ways of running a flow need the **Run Flows** user permission. Give it in a profile or permission set. A flow on a Lightning page starts every time the page loads.

A screen flow can't use a **Wait** element (a pause until a time or event). And a record-triggered flow can't show screens. If a person must answer, it's a screen flow, launched from a button or page.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Screen = a person. Put it where the person already is**: the record page, a button or the utility bar.

terms.say: A flow that shows screens to a person and asks them questions, one step at a time.
One save job. Everything in it succeeds together, or it all gets undone together.
A page built with Lightning App Builder, like a record, home or app page.
A button on a record that opens a screen flow. It is a kind of quick action.
A thin strip at the bottom of a Lightning app with handy tools that stay open.
The tool for building sites and portals for customers, partners or visitors.
A flow variable name. On a record page, Salesforce puts the record's Id into it so the flow knows where it is.
A tick on a flow variable that lets the outside world pass a value in when the flow starts.
A user permission that lets people run flows.
A flow element that pauses until a time or an event. Screen flows can't use it.

lessons.title: Scheduled and autolaunched flows, subflows
lessons.objective: Create and configure flows using Flow Builder.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Some flows run with nobody watching. A **schedule-triggered flow** runs at a set time for a group of records. An **autolaunched flow** runs when something calls it. A **subflow** lets one flow call another, so you build a piece once and reuse it.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A dishwasher on a timer (scheduled) and a kettle you switch on (autolaunched). A subflow is a recipe card one recipe points to: "make the sauce from card 12." Where it stops: none of these can show a screen on their own.

cards.title: Schedule-triggered flows
items: Run **once, daily or weekly** at a start time
Pick an object and filters; one **interview** (one run) per record in `$Record`
At most **250,000 interviews per 24 hours**, or 200 × user licenses if higher
Watch them on the **Scheduled Jobs** page in Setup

cards.title: Autolaunched (no trigger) flows
items: Called by Apex, the REST API, a custom button or link, or a subflow
No screens and no choices
Great as a reusable **subflow** for logic many flows share

cards.title: Transactions
cards.body: Flows run inside a transaction. If something fails, the **whole transaction rolls back** (all its changes are undone). A called flow shares the caller's limits, like 100 queries and 150 saves per transaction. Going over a limit rolls back even with a fault path.
"Every night, update all overdue invoices" is a schedule-triggered flow, not a record-triggered one. Nothing is being saved at midnight, so a record trigger never fires.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Clock, caller or child.** Clock = scheduled. Caller = autolaunched. Child = subflow.

terms.say: A flow that wakes up at a set time and works through a group of records.
A flow with no screens that runs in the background when something calls it.
A flow that another flow calls, like a helper that does one job for many flows.
One run of a flow. If a flow runs for 10 records, that's 10 interviews.
The most scheduled flow runs an org gets in a day, unless 200 times its user licenses is bigger.
A Setup page that lists jobs waiting to run later, including scheduled flows.
A way for other systems to call Salesforce over the web.
If one part fails, every change in that save job is undone, as if it never happened.

lessons.title: Flow Approval processes
lessons.objective: Describe the capabilities and use cases for Flow Approval processes.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: An **approval** means someone must say yes before a record moves on, like a manager approving a big discount. **Flow Approval Processes** let you build multi-step, multi-user approvals in Flow Builder. They are a kind of orchestration made of **stages** and **steps**.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A permission slip passed along a line: teacher, then head teacher, then a parent. Each one signs or says no. Where it stops: some stages can ask several people at once, not just one after another.

cards.title: Two types
items: **Autolaunched Flow Approval Process**: started by Apex, the REST API, or a custom button or link
It has the inputs `recordId`, `submitter` and `submissionComments`
**Record-Triggered Flow Approval Process**: starts after save when a record is created or updated

cards.title: Building blocks
items: **Approval step**: asks a user, group or queue to approve or reject
**Background step**: runs an autolaunched flow, like a field update or email
**Recall path**: what runs if the submitter pulls the request back
Custom emails come from **text templates**

cards.title: Locking the record
cards.body: While a record is under review it can be **locked**, so others can't edit it. For approval steps that run one after another, tick **Lock the record** in the step. For steps that run at the same time, lock and unlock with background steps instead, because a record can hold only one lock.

cards.title: Limits and the classic tool
cards.body: Per org: **50 versions** per flow approval process, **2,000 active** and **4,000 total**. The classic **Approval Processes** tool still exists. In Flow, approvers are set in the process, so the submitter can't pick an approver by hand.
A record-triggered flow approval process needs no Submit for Approval button: saving a matching record starts it. To start one from a button, use the autolaunched type.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Stages hold steps. Steps ask people. Background steps do the chores.**

terms.say: A yes-or-no check by a chosen person before a record can move on.
Approvals you build in Flow Builder, with stages and steps for many people.
Big chunks of an approval, done in order. Each stage holds one or more steps.
A step that asks a person, group or queue to approve or reject the record.
A step that does a job by itself, like updating a field, by running an autolaunched flow.
What the approval does if the person who sent it takes it back.
Reusable text with blanks that fill in from the flow, used for custom emails.
A locked record can't be edited by most users while it waits for approval.
The person who sent the record for approval.
The older Setup tool for approvals. It still works, next to approvals built in Flow.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Flows can fail, for example when a validation rule blocks an Update Records element. Good admins plan for it. Add **fault paths**, test before you activate, and know where to look when something breaks.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A sat-nav with a detour. If a road is closed, the fault path is the detour you planned. Where it stops: a detour can't save you from running out of fuel. Going over a governor limit still undoes everything.

cards.title: Fault paths
cards.body: A **fault path** is an extra route from an element that runs if that element fails. Use it to email an admin, show a friendly message in a screen flow, or log the problem. With no fault path, the **default error handling** applies, and the user sees a general error.

cards.title: Error emails
cards.body: By default, the error email goes to the **user who last modified the flow**. In **Process Automation Settings** you can send it to the **Apex Exception Email Recipients** list instead.

cards.title: Testing with Debug
items: **Debug** in Flow Builder runs the flow and shows each step
It really saves data unless you choose **rollback mode**
**Debug as another user** works only in a sandbox (a test copy of your org)
You need the **View All Data** permission

cards.title: Keeping flows healthy
items: Only one version of a flow is **active**; edit by saving a new version
Compare versions and see what calls a flow in the Automation app
Check paused interviews and scheduled jobs in Setup

cards.body: A fault path does not stop a **governor limit** error (a hard cap like 100 queries per transaction). The whole transaction rolls back anyway, so fix the design: no Get Records or Update Records inside a loop.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Plan the detour, test in rollback, read the email.**

terms.say: An extra route a flow takes when a step fails, so you can handle the error kindly.
What Salesforce does when a step fails and there's no fault path: show a general error and maybe undo the save.

terms.term: user who last modified the flow
terms.say: The person who most recently saved changes to the flow. By default they get its error emails.
A Setup page with settings for flows, like who gets flow error emails.
A list in Setup of people who get error emails. Flow error emails can go there too.
A Flow Builder button that runs the flow as a test and shows every step it takes.
A Debug option that undoes every change when the test run ends, so no real data is saved.
A copy of your org for building and testing, so real data stays safe.
A strong permission that lets a user see every record in the org.
A hard cap Salesforce sets, like 100 queries per transaction, so one org can't hog shared servers.

lessons.title: Agentforce for business automation
lessons.objective: Describe the capabilities and use cases for using Agentforce to automate business processes.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **Agentforce** adds AI **agents** to Salesforce. An agent understands requests in everyday words, then picks and runs actions to get the job done. Admins use it two ways: agents that help users and customers, and **Setup with Agentforce** that helps admins themselves.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A smart helper at a front desk. You say what you need; it knows which forms to fill and which colleague to call. Where it stops: it can only use the tools (actions) you give it.

cards.title: How an agent is built
items: **Topics**: the jobs it handles, each with **instructions**
**Actions**: what it can do
Custom actions can be built from a **flow**, an **Apex invocable method** or a **prompt template**

cards.title: Setup with Agentforce
cards.body: **Setup with Agentforce** is an agent inside Setup. You ask in plain words. It can create objects, fields, flows and formulas, and manage permission sets, sharing rules and org-wide defaults. It acts **only after you approve**. It works **only within your own permissions**.

cards.title: Tracking and grounding
cards.body: Every change the Setup agent makes is logged in the **Setup Audit Trail**. A **Prompt Template Capability-Triggered Flow** adds data to a prompt template, so the AI's answer uses your records.

An agent doesn't replace flows. Use a flow for a fixed, rule-based process that must run the same way every time. Use an agent when requests come in free text and the next step depends on what was asked. The agent can then call your flow as an action.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Flows follow the map. Agents read the question, then pick the road.**

terms.say: Salesforce's AI helpers. They understand everyday words and can take actions for you.
AI helpers that read a request, decide what to do and run actions to do it.
An AI helper inside Setup. You ask in plain words, and after you say yes it builds or changes things for you.
The jobs an agent knows how to handle, like order questions or bookings.
Plain-word rules that tell an agent how to behave for a topic.
The things an agent can actually do, like run a flow or look up an order.
A piece of Apex code marked so flows and agents can call it like a ready-made action.
A saved set of instructions for the AI, with blanks that fill in from your records.
A history log of changes made in Setup: who changed what, and when.

flashcards.front: Can a user type a value into a formula field?
flashcards.back: No. A formula field is read-only. Salesforce works out its value from other fields every time the record is read.

flashcards.front: What are a formula's size limits?
flashcards.back: Up to 3,900 characters typed, 1,300 characters displayed after it runs, and 15,000 bytes for save size and compile size.

flashcards.front: How do you compare a picklist in a formula?
flashcards.back: Use `ISPICKVAL(field, "Value")` or `TEXT(field)`. A plain `=` comparison on a picklist doesn't work.

flashcards.front: Which return types can a formula have?
flashcards.back: Checkbox, Currency, Date, Date/Time, Number, Percent, Text and Time.

flashcards.front: Which way can a cross-object formula read?
flashcards.back: Up only, to parent records, like `Account.Industry`. To summarize child records, use a roll-up summary or a flow.

flashcards.front: How many unique relationships can one object use in cross-object formulas?
flashcards.back: 10. The count covers all formulas, rules and lookup filters on the object. The same path used twice counts once.

flashcards.front: How do you read the owner when a queue can own the record?
flashcards.back: Name the type: `Owner:User.` for a person or `Owner:Queue.` for a queue.

flashcards.front: What can a roll-up summary field calculate?
flashcards.back: COUNT of child records, or the SUM, MIN or MAX of a child field. SUM needs number, currency or percent. MIN and MAX also take dates.

flashcards.front: Where can you create roll-up summary fields?
flashcards.back: On the master of a master-detail. Also Account from opportunities, Opportunity from opportunity products and Campaign from campaign members.

flashcards.front: What can't a roll-up summary aggregate?
flashcards.back: Auto number fields, cross-object formulas, and formulas using `NOW()`, `TODAY()` or `DATEVALUE()`.

flashcards.front: What happens to a master-detail once a roll-up summary uses it?
flashcards.back: You can't convert it to a lookup or change the detail object. Delete the roll-up first.

flashcards.front: When does a validation rule block a save?
flashcards.back: When its formula returns TRUE. The formula describes the bad data, then the error shows at the top of the page or next to a field.

flashcards.front: Do validation rules run for API saves and imports?
flashcards.back: Yes, even for fields not on the layout. The exception is Quick Create.

flashcards.front: How do you let chosen users skip a validation rule?
flashcards.back: Give them a custom permission in a permission set. In the rule, add `NOT($Permission.Your_Permission)`.

flashcards.front: Which functions make a rule fire only when needed?
flashcards.back: `ISNEW()` for new records, `ISCHANGED(field)` for a changed field, and `PRIORVALUE(field)` for the old value.

flashcards.front: Which flow type asks a person for input?
flashcards.back: A screen flow. It's the only type that shows screens and uses Choice resources.

flashcards.front: Which flow type runs at a set time for many records?
flashcards.back: A schedule-triggered flow. It runs once, daily or weekly, with one interview per matching record.

flashcards.front: Which element is only for record-triggered flows?
flashcards.back: The Custom Error element. It rolls back the change and shows your message on the page or next to a field.

flashcards.front: What is an orchestration?
flashcards.back: A multi-step, multi-user process in Flow, made of stages and steps. People get screen flows; background steps run automation.

flashcards.front: When should you use a before-save flow?
flashcards.back: To update fields on the record that triggered it. It's the fastest choice. It can use only Assignment, Decision, Get Records and Loop.

flashcards.front: When do you need an after-save flow?
flashcards.back: To create or update related records, run actions like emails, or use the new record's Id.

flashcards.front: What does "only when a record is updated to meet the condition requirements" do?
flashcards.back: The flow runs only when the record changes from not matching to matching. Later edits that still match don't run it.

flashcards.front: How many versions can a flow have?
flashcards.back: Up to 50 versions, and only one is active. Orgs get 2,000 active and 4,000 total flows per flow type.

flashcards.front: How does a screen flow know which record it's on?
flashcards.back: Create a text variable named `recordId` and mark it Available for input. Record pages and flow actions fill it in.

flashcards.front: Where can users launch a screen flow?
flashcards.back: Lightning pages, flow actions, the utility bar, custom buttons and links, Experience Builder pages, and inside LWC, Aura or Visualforce.

flashcards.front: Which permission do most users need to run a flow?
flashcards.back: Run Flows. Give it in a profile or permission set.

flashcards.front: What is the daily limit for schedule-triggered flow interviews?
flashcards.back: 250,000 per 24 hours, or 200 × user licenses, whichever is greater.

flashcards.front: What happens when a flow breaks a governor limit?
flashcards.back: The whole transaction rolls back, even if the element has a fault path.

flashcards.front: What can start an autolaunched flow with no trigger?
flashcards.back: Apex, the REST API, custom buttons or links, web tabs, Visualforce, or another flow as a subflow.

flashcards.front: What are the two flow approval process types?
flashcards.back: Autolaunched (started by Apex, REST API, buttons or links) and record-triggered after save (on create or update).

flashcards.front: How do you lock a record during concurrent approval steps?
flashcards.back: Use background steps that call the Lock Record action. The step's Lock the record setting can't be used, because a record holds only one lock.

flashcards.front: What happens when a flow approval is recalled?
flashcards.back: The running stage and open work items are canceled. The recall path's stage runs, then the submission is recalled.

flashcards.front: Who gets flow error emails?
flashcards.back: By default, the user who last modified the flow. Process Automation Settings can send them to Apex Exception Email Recipients instead.

flashcards.front: Does Debug in Flow Builder change real data?
flashcards.back: Yes, unless you choose rollback mode. Closing a run doesn't undo changes already made.

flashcards.front: Where can you debug a flow as another user?
flashcards.back: Only in a sandbox, after a one-time setup. Debugging needs View All Data.

flashcards.front: What is a fault path for?
flashcards.back: It's the route a flow takes when an element fails. Use it to email an admin, show a friendly screen or log the error.

flashcards.front: What can Setup with Agentforce do?
flashcards.back: Create objects, fields, flows and formulas, and manage permission sets and sharing. It acts only after you approve, within your permissions.

flashcards.front: What can a custom agent action be built from?
flashcards.back: A flow, an Apex invocable method or a prompt template.

flashcards.front: When is a flow better than an agent?
flashcards.back: When the process follows fixed rules and must run the same way every time. Agents fit free-text requests.

questions.q: A sales manager wants each opportunity to show its amount after a 10% discount. Nobody should be able to type over the value. What should the app builder create?
options: A formula field that returns Currency
A currency field filled in by users
A roll-up summary field on Opportunity
A validation rule on the Amount field
questions.explain: A formula field calculates its value from other fields and is read-only. Return type Currency fits a money amount.
wrong: Users could type any value, and nothing keeps it in step with the amount.
A roll-up summarizes child records. This value comes from the record's own field.
A validation rule blocks bad saves. It doesn't calculate or show a value.

questions.q: Which statement about formula fields is true?
options: Users can edit the value when they need to override it
The value is calculated once when the record is created
The value is calculated from other fields and can't be edited
They can only return Text or Number values
questions.explain: A formula field is read-only. Salesforce works out its value from other fields each time the record is read.
wrong: Formula fields are read-only. Nobody can type into them.
A formula recalculates whenever the record is viewed, so it stays current.
Formulas can also return Checkbox, Currency, Date, Date/Time, Percent and Time.

questions.q: What is the most characters you can type into one formula?
options: 1,300 characters
3,900 characters
5,000 characters
15,000 characters
questions.explain: A formula can hold up to 3,900 characters. Separate limits cover what it displays (1,300 characters) and its compiled size (15,000 bytes).
wrong: 1,300 is the most a text formula can display after it runs.
That isn't a formula limit.
15,000 is the byte limit for save and compile size, not characters typed.

questions.q: A support team wants a Case field that shows a red flag image when a case is more than 3 days old and still open. Which return type should the formula use?
options: Checkbox
Percent
Date
Text
questions.explain: To show a picture, the formula returns Text and uses the `IMAGE()` function. Checkbox can only show a tick.
wrong: A checkbox shows only a tick. It can't show a picture of a flag.
A percent formula shows a number with a % sign, not a picture.
A date formula returns a date, not a flag.
questions.source: Formula Operators and Functions by Context

questions.q: A formula on a custom object fails to save with a syntax error. What is wrong?
options: Text formulas can't compare picklist fields at all
The formula needs `ISNEW()` before it can test a field
`IF()` needs four arguments in a text formula
A picklist must be checked with `ISPICKVAL()` or `TEXT()`, not compared with `=`
questions.explain: Picklists aren't plain text in formulas. Use `ISPICKVAL(Status__c, "Closed")` or `TEXT(Status__c)` to compare them.
wrong: They can. Wrap the picklist in `TEXT()` or use `ISPICKVAL()`.
`ISNEW()` isn't available in formula fields, and no test needs it.
`IF()` takes three: the test, the true value and the false value.
questions.source: Formula Operators and Functions by Context

questions.q: An admin tries to delete a custom field, `Tier__c`, but Salesforce stops them. Two formula fields use it. What must the admin do first?
options: Deactivate both formula fields
Remove `Tier__c` from both formulas
Remove `Tier__c` from every page layout
Ask Salesforce Support to force the delete
questions.explain: You can't delete a field that a formula references. Take it out of the formulas, then delete it.
wrong: Formula fields can't be deactivated. The reference must be removed.
Page layouts don't block deletion. The formula references do.
Support isn't needed. Removing the references is enough.

questions.q: Which field types can't be referenced inside a formula field? (Choose 2)
options: Long text area fields
Encrypted fields
Picklist fields
Date fields
Lookup fields
questions.explain: Formulas can't use long text area, encrypted or Description fields. Picklists, dates and lookups all work.
wrong: Picklists can be used through `ISPICKVAL()` or `TEXT()`.
Date fields are common in formulas, for example `Due_Date__c - TODAY()`.
A lookup lets a formula read the related record's fields.

questions.q: A text formula on Account joins many fields into one long summary. Users see it cut short on the page. Which limit is it hitting?
options: 1,300 characters displayed after evaluation
3,900 characters of formula text
15,000 bytes of compile size
255 characters for any text field
questions.explain: A formula can display at most 1,300 characters after it runs. A longer result is cut short.
wrong: That limits what you type into the formula, not what it shows.
Compile size stops the formula from saving. It doesn't cut off the result.
Text formulas can show more than 255 characters.

questions.q: An admin saves this formula on Case. Salesforce rejects it with a compile size error, even though it has fewer than 3,900 characters. What is the most likely reason?
questions.code:
CASE(Region_Formula__c,
  "EMEA", DATEVALUE(Promise_Time__c) + 3,
  "APAC", DATEVALUE(Promise_Time__c) + 5,
  DATEVALUE(Promise_Time__c) + 7)

// Region_Formula__c is itself a long formula field
options: The formula references a field from the parent account
`CASE()` can only compare up to five values
Referenced formulas and functions like `DATEVALUE()` add to the compile size
Text formulas must stay under 1,300 characters before they save
questions.explain: Compile size counts the expanded formula, including other formula fields it uses. Functions like `TEXT()`, `DATE()`, `DATEVALUE()` and `DATETIMEVALUE()` grow it. The limit is 15,000 bytes.
wrong: Cross-object fields are allowed. They don't usually cause a size error on their own.
`CASE()` has no five-value limit.
1,300 is the display limit after it runs, not a save limit.

questions.q: Ivy Lane Books wants a field showing the days left until an order's promised date. It must be correct every morning without any automation running. Which solution meets this?
options: A number field updated by a nightly schedule-triggered flow
A number formula field: `Promised_Date__c - TODAY()`
A roll-up summary that takes the MIN of the promised date
A validation rule that compares the date with `TODAY()`
questions.explain: A formula recalculates every time the record is read, so `TODAY()` is always current. No scheduled job is needed.
wrong: It works but adds automation the requirement wants to avoid, and is stale between runs.
A roll-up summarizes child records, and can't use `TODAY()`.
A validation rule blocks saves. It doesn't store or show a value.

questions.q: A manager asks for an Opportunity field that shows what the stage was before the latest edit. A teammate suggests this formula field. What happens?
options: It can't be saved, because `PRIORVALUE()` isn't available in formula fields
It saves and shows the old stage after each edit
It saves, but always shows the current stage
It works only if field history tracking is on for Stage
questions.explain: `PRIORVALUE()` and `ISCHANGED()` work in validation rules and flow formulas, not formula fields. To keep the old value, a record-triggered flow can copy it into a normal field.
wrong: Formula fields can't use `PRIORVALUE()`.
It doesn't save in the first place.
History tracking doesn't make `PRIORVALUE()` available in formula fields.
questions.source: Formula Operators and Functions by Context

questions.q: A company wants a Contact field that shows "VIP" when the contact's lifetime spend is over 50,000, and lets account managers override it to "VIP" by hand. Which design meets both needs?
options: A text formula field that returns "VIP" from the spend
A roll-up summary field with a filter on spend
A validation rule that requires "VIP" when spend is high
A picklist set by a record-triggered flow when spend passes 50,000
questions.explain: A formula field can't be edited, so a manual override needs a normal field. A flow can set it automatically, and users can still change it.
wrong: Users can't override a formula, so the manual part fails.
A roll-up can't be typed into, and Contact isn't a master here.
A rule blocks saves. It doesn't fill in the value.

questions.q: A contact record should show its account's phone number, always up to date. What is the simplest solution?
options: A roll-up summary field on Contact
A record-triggered flow that copies the phone
A cross-object formula: `Account.Phone`
A lookup filter on the Account field
questions.explain: A cross-object formula reads a parent's field with dot notation. It always shows the current value.
wrong: Roll-ups live on the parent and summarize children. Contact isn't the master here.
It works but needs extra automation, and copies can go out of date.
A lookup filter limits which records you can pick. It doesn't show values.

questions.q: In which direction can a cross-object formula read data?
options: Up, from a record to its related parent records
Down, from a parent to its child records
Sideways, to any record with the same name
Both up and down, if the link is master-detail
questions.explain: Cross-object formulas follow relationships up to parents, like `Account.Industry`. To summarize children, use a roll-up summary.
wrong: Formulas can't read child records. That's what roll-ups do.
Formulas follow relationship fields, not matching names.
Even with master-detail, a formula only reads up.

questions.q: How many unique relationships can one object use in cross-object formulas?
options: 5, counted per formula field
15, counted across all its formula fields only
10, counted across all its formulas, rules and lookup filters
There is no limit on relationships
questions.explain: Each object can use at most 10 unique relationships. The count covers formula fields, rules and lookup filters together.
wrong: The limit is 10, and it's counted across all formulas, rules and lookup filters.
It's 10, and validation rules and lookup filters count too.
Salesforce allows at most 10 unique relationships per object.

questions.q: Two formula fields on Opportunity read `Account.Industry` and `Account.Rating`. A validation rule on Opportunity reads `Account.Owner.Email`. How many unique relationships do these use?
options: One
Two
Three
Four
questions.explain: Repeated paths count once. Opportunity to Account is one. Account to its Owner is a second.
wrong: The path through the account owner is a second relationship.
The two `Account.` formulas share one relationship, so they count once.
Repeated paths count once, so the total is lower.

questions.q: A Lead formula must show the owner's email. Leads can be owned by users or queues. Which formula is right?
options: `Owner.Email`
`Owner:Group.Email`
`$User.Email`
`IF(ISBLANK(Owner:User.Id), Owner:Queue.QueueEmail, Owner:User.Email)`
questions.explain: On objects that queues can own, Owner can point to a user or a queue. Name the type with `Owner:User.` or `Owner:Queue.`.
wrong: On objects with queues, Owner is polymorphic, so you must name the type.
There's no `Owner:Group.` path. Use `Owner:User.` or `Owner:Queue.`.
`$User` is the person viewing the record, not the record's owner.

questions.q: Which statements about cross-object formulas are true? (Choose 2)
options: They can read fields from child records
They copy the parent's value at save time
They can't be used as the field a roll-up summary adds up
They only work on master-detail relationships
Task and event formulas can't use contact or account merge fields
questions.explain: You can't reference cross-object formulas in roll-up summaries. Activities can't reach related contact or account merge fields.
wrong: They only read up to parent records.
They read the parent's current value when the record is viewed.
They work on lookups too.

questions.q: Harbor Rentals wants each Booking to show the name of its account's owner. The admin writes this formula, but Salesforce won't let them pick the field. Why?
options: Bookings can't reach the account's owner, because it's two relationships away
Cross-object formulas can't read from standard objects
The formula must be a roll-up summary instead
Name fields built from other fields, like the owner's Name, can't be used
questions.explain: Name fields made from other fields can't be used in formulas, such as `Owner.Name`. Use `FirstName & " " & LastName` instead.
wrong: Formulas can go many levels up. Distance isn't the problem.
They read standard objects like Account all the time.
A roll-up summarizes children. This reads up to a parent.

questions.q: An Invoice object has a lookup to Account. The finance team wants Account to show the total of all invoice amounts, and also wants each invoice to show the account's credit limit. Which two features meet these needs? (Choose 2)
options: A cross-object formula on Account that adds up invoice amounts
A cross-object formula on Invoice for the credit limit
A roll-up summary field on Invoice
A record-triggered flow on Invoice that updates the account total
A validation rule on Account that totals the invoices
questions.explain: A formula on the child reads the parent's credit limit. With a lookup, not master-detail, a flow can keep the parent total up to date.
wrong: Formulas can't read down to child records.
A roll-up lives on the parent and sums children. Invoice is the child.
Validation rules check data. They don't store totals.

questions.q: An Opportunity object already uses 10 unique relationships in its formulas, rules and lookup filters. An admin adds a new formula that reads `Account.Owner.Manager.Email`, a path no other formula uses. What happens?
options: It saves, because limits apply only to validation rules
It fails to save, because it adds unique relationships past the limit of 10
It saves, but the value shows as blank
It saves, because each formula field has its own 10
questions.explain: The 10-relationship limit is per object and cumulative. A new, unused path adds to it, so the formula won't save.
wrong: The limit counts formula fields too.
Salesforce blocks the save. It doesn't show a blank value.
The 10 is per object, across everything that uses relationships.

questions.q: Which four calculations can a roll-up summary field do?
options: COUNT, SUM, MIN and MAX
COUNT, SUM, AVERAGE and MAX
SUM, AVERAGE, MEDIAN and MIN
COUNT, SUM, FIRST and LAST
questions.explain: Roll-ups can COUNT children, or find the SUM, MIN or MAX of a child field.
wrong: There's no AVERAGE roll-up. A formula can divide SUM by COUNT.
AVERAGE and MEDIAN aren't roll-up types.
FIRST and LAST aren't roll-up types.

questions.q: In a master-detail relationship, where do you create the roll-up summary field?
options: On the detail object
On a junction object between them
On the master object
On a report type for both objects
questions.explain: A roll-up summary is a field on the master. It summarizes the master's detail records.
wrong: The detail is what gets counted. The total lives above it.
No junction object is needed for a roll-up.
A report type is for reports. A roll-up is a field.

questions.q: On which standard objects can you create roll-up summary fields from standard child objects? (Choose 2)
options: Account, summarizing its opportunities
Contact, summarizing its cases
Case, summarizing its case comments
Lead, summarizing its tasks
Opportunity, summarizing its opportunity products
questions.explain: Standard roll-ups exist for Account from opportunities, Opportunity from opportunity products and Campaign from campaign members.
wrong: Contact isn't on that list.
Case isn't on that list.
Lead isn't on that list.

questions.q: A roll-up summary must show the latest Delivery Date among an order's lines. Which roll-up type and field fit?
options: SUM of the Delivery Date field
MAX of the Delivery Date field
COUNT with a Delivery Date filter
MIN of the Delivery Date field
questions.explain: MIN and MAX work on date and date/time fields. MAX gives the latest date.
wrong: SUM works only on number, currency and percent fields.
COUNT gives how many, not a date.
MIN finds the earliest date, not the latest.

questions.q: A Project object is the master of Task Item records. The manager wants to see how many task items are still open. What should the admin build?
options: A COUNT roll-up summary with filter criteria Status not equal to Done
A SUM roll-up summary on the Status field
A cross-object formula on Project reading `Task_Item__r.Status__c`
A COUNT roll-up summary on Task Item
questions.explain: A COUNT roll-up on the master can use filter criteria to count only some children.
wrong: SUM adds number fields. Status is a picklist.
Formulas can't read down to children.
The roll-up goes on the master, Project, not the detail.

questions.q: An admin built a roll-up summary on Shipment from its Package records. Now the team wants to change the relationship to a lookup. What happens?
options: Salesforce converts it and deletes the roll-up for you
The conversion works and the roll-up keeps calculating
The conversion works only in a sandbox
The conversion is blocked while the roll-up summary exists
questions.explain: After a roll-up summary is created, you can't convert its master-detail into a lookup. Delete the roll-up first.
wrong: Salesforce won't convert it while the roll-up exists.
Roll-ups can't keep working on a lookup.
The rule is the same in every org.

questions.q: Which fields can't be the field a roll-up summary aggregates? (Choose 2)
options: A currency field
A number formula with no cross-object references
An auto number field
A formula field that uses `TODAY()`
A date field
questions.explain: Auto numbers can't be aggregated. Formulas using `NOW()`, `TODAY()` or `DATEVALUE()`, or cross-object references, aren't allowed either.
wrong: Currency fields work with SUM, MIN and MAX.
A formula without on-the-fly functions or cross-object references can be summarized.
Date fields work with MIN and MAX.

questions.q: A Trip object is the master of Booking records. Trips may hold at most 25 bookings. Trip has a roll-up `Booking_Count__c`. Where should the validation rule go, and which formula works?
options: On Trip: `Booking_Count__c >= 25`
On Booking: `Trip__r.Booking_Count__c > 25`
On Booking: `AND(ISNEW(), Trip__r.Booking_Count__c >= 25)`
On Trip: `AND(ISNEW(), Booking_Count__c >= 25)`
questions.explain: To cap children, put the rule on the child. Check `ISNEW()` and whether the parent's count already reached the cap.
wrong: This blocks the 25th booking, and any edit to a full trip.
This fires on every edit and only after 26 exist, so it's too late.
A new Trip has no bookings yet, so this never helps.

questions.q: A finance admin changes the expression of a formula field that a roll-up summary uses. Thousands of parent records must recalculate. Which statements are true? (Choose 2)
options: Every parent record is blocked from editing until it finishes
The recalculation can take up to 30 minutes
The mass recalculation fires validation rules on each parent
The admin must start the recalculation from Data Loader
The mass recalculation doesn't fire workflow rules or validation rules
questions.explain: Changing a formula a roll-up uses causes a mass recalculation. It can take up to 30 minutes and doesn't fire workflow or validation rules.
wrong: No such block exists.
A mass recalculation doesn't trigger workflow or validation rules.
Salesforce starts it by itself.

questions.q: Field-level security hides the `Cost__c` field on Expense Line from most users. Expense Report has a SUM roll-up of `Cost__c`. What do those users see on the report's total?
options: A total that includes every line's cost
A total that leaves out lines they can't see
A blank total, because they can't see `Cost__c`
An error saying they lack access
questions.explain: Fields hidden by field-level security on the detail are still included in the roll-up. Protect the roll-up field itself if the total is secret.
wrong: Hidden fields still count.
The total still shows. Its own security decides that.
No error appears.

questions.q: A Warehouse is the master of Bin records. Bin has a formula field `Location_Label__c` that reads `Warehouse__r.City__c`. The admin wants a roll-up that counts bins where that label equals "Austin". What happens?
options: It works, because COUNT ignores formula fields
It works, but only after a mass recalculation
It can't be built, because roll-up filters can't use cross-object formula fields
It can't be built, because COUNT can't have filter criteria
questions.explain: Roll-up filters can't use cross-object formula fields. Filter on a normal field instead.
wrong: Filters still can't use a cross-object formula.
Recalculation doesn't change what the filter allows.
COUNT can have filters. The cross-object formula is the problem.

questions.q: How many roll-up summary fields can one object have by default?
questions.explain: The default allocation is 25 roll-up summary fields per object.
wrong: That's the cross-object relationship limit, a different rule.
40 is the default for relationship fields, not roll-ups.
100 is far above the roll-up allocation.

questions.q: When does a validation rule block a save?
options: When its formula returns FALSE
When the record has a blank required field
Only when a user saves from a page layout
When its formula returns TRUE
questions.explain: A validation rule's formula describes bad data. TRUE means invalid, so the save stops and the error shows.
wrong: FALSE means the data is fine, so the save goes on.
That's a required field check, not a validation rule.
Rules also run for the API and imports.

questions.q: Where can a validation rule's error message appear?
options: Only in an email to the record owner
Only in the debug log
In a pop-up after the record saves
At the top of the page or next to a field
questions.explain: You choose: the top of the page, or next to a specific field.
wrong: The message shows on the screen, not in an email.
Users see the message on the page.
The record doesn't save. The message shows instead.

questions.q: In which situation does a validation rule NOT run?
options: A record is saved through the API
A record is created with Quick Create
The checked field isn't on the page layout
Data is loaded with the Data Import Wizard
questions.explain: Validation rules check new and changed records everywhere, including the API and imports. Quick Create is the exception.
wrong: Validation rules run for API saves.
Rules still run when the field isn't on the layout.
Imports are checked too.

questions.q: The rule should be: "Discount can't be more than 20%." Which formula is correct?
options: `Discount__c > 0.20`
`Discount__c <= 0.20`
`NOT(Discount__c > 0.20)`
`ISCHANGED(Discount__c)`
questions.explain: Write the bad case. A percent of 20% is stored as 0.20, so `Discount__c > 0.20` returns TRUE when it's too high.
wrong: This is the good case. It would block every valid discount.
This returns TRUE for valid discounts, so it blocks them.
This blocks every change, not just large discounts.

questions.q: This validation rule is on Opportunity. When does it block a save?
options: Whenever the stage is Closed Won
When Amount is empty on any stage
When the stage is Closed Won and Amount is empty
Never, because `ISBLANK()` can't check currency fields
questions.explain: `AND()` is TRUE only when both parts are TRUE. So it blocks Closed Won deals that have no amount.
wrong: It also needs the amount to be blank.
It only fires for Closed Won.
`ISBLANK()` works on number and currency fields.

questions.q: A rule should fire only when someone edits the Close Date, not when other fields change. Which function helps?
options: `ISNEW()`
`ISCHANGED(CloseDate)`
`PRIORVALUE(Amount)`
`TODAY()`
questions.explain: `ISCHANGED(field)` returns TRUE only when that field changed in this save.
wrong: `ISNEW()` is TRUE only on create.
This returns the old amount. It doesn't check the close date.
`TODAY()` gives the date. It doesn't detect a change.

questions.q: An integration user must load records that break a validation rule. Everyone else must still be checked. What is the best approach?
options: Add a custom permission check, such as `NOT($Permission.Skip_Rules)`, and give the permission in a permission set
Deactivate the rule during each load
Check `$Profile.Name` against the integration profile name
Move the rule into a page layout
questions.explain: Bypass a rule with a custom permission checked through `$Permission`. Assign it only to the users who need to skip it.
wrong: Others could save bad data while it's off.
It works but is brittle. A custom permission is the recommended pattern.
Page layouts can't hold validation rules.

questions.q: Which statements about validation rules are true? (Choose 2)
options: They can check fields on a parent record through a relationship
They run only when a user saves from a Lightning page
`VLOOKUP()` can be used only in validation rules
They return FALSE to block a save
They only run when the record is first created
questions.explain: Validation rules can use cross-object references, like `Account.Rating`. `VLOOKUP()` is available only in validation rules.
wrong: They also run for the API and imports.
TRUE blocks the save.
They run on create and on every update.
